rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes the untrellised produce as creepers growing horizontally along the ground, such as melons, watermelons, and cucumbers.
rows.anchor: refers to creepers which grow and develop horizontally along the surface of the earth like melons, water-melons and cucumbers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads the paired terms in 80:28 as grapes and fresh vegetables.
rows.anchor: The former refers to grapes and the latter to vegetables that are eaten while being fresh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abundant variety beyond what survival requires displays the Creator's generosity and mercy and should awaken gratitude and recognition of people's obligations to God.
rows.anchor: the Creator of this world embellished it with such an innumerable range of products for us

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Receiving divine blessings entails accountability: God will question people and reward or punish them, since every privilege brings responsibility.
rows.anchor: That both necessitate one another is an obvious fact of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diversity and harmony of creation point to one Creator and governor, and invite reflection on divine provision matching human needs and senses.
rows.anchor: unity in multiplicity, harmony in diversity, accord in discord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The varied produce is evidence for monotheism and the hereafter, directing attention from diversity to the Creator's oneness; he refers back to 6:99-101.
rows.anchor: This aspect points to the Creator of this universe and to the oneness of its governor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enjoying ripe fruit and giving its due at harvest follows from God's favors, prophetic teaching, and uncorrupted human nature.
rows.anchor: benefit from these fruits when they ripen and give away what is due of it upon the day of its harvest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to God or the fruit without changing the point: gratitude requires sharing a divine favor with those who lack it, an innate right called God's right.
rows.anchor: Every favour of God necessarily entails that he who receives it must also share it with others who are without it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He traces the innate duty of giving to Abel's offering and says formal zakāh was instituted in Israelite and Ishmaelite law.
rows.anchor: The offering of his livestock to the Almighty made by Adam’s son Abel was for this very purpose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the due is gratitude for the farmer's harvest, zakāh should be paid when produce is harvested; he says taxation instead of zakāh is un-Islamic and unjust.
rows.anchor: this right should be discharged at the time of the harvest from the produce

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular pronoun can refer to every listed crop individually, so zakāh applies to all kinds of produce subject to an exemption tied to the producer's needs.
rows.anchor: in Islam God has a right in every produce whatever the thing; only a certain amount is exempt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cannot understand jurists' exclusion of certain produce from zakāh, except where small household amounts justify exemption.
rows.anchor: Jurists do not regard certain entities to zakatable, which is beyond my comprehension

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording supports levying zakāh on what is produced and collected for use, not on land as a means of production.
rows.anchor: zakāh is to be imposed on production and not on the land which is a means of production

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on excess after giving produce's due is needed because moderation and frugality let people meet others' rights.
rows.anchor: the fulfilment of rights is based on a person being moderate and frugal in his needs and desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan draws the wealthy into luxuries until their animals live well while their hungry neighbours receive no share.
rows.anchor: dogs, falcons and hawks of such people live in luxury while their neighbours sleep in hunger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tall quadrupeds are animals fit for transport and carrying loads, including camels, horses, and mules.
rows.anchor: appropriate as means transport and as a beasts of burden like camels, horses and mules etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for the shorter category refers to fertile or not-yet-sprouted land and to short animals kept for slaughter and other uses rather than transport or carrying loads.
rows.anchor: those short statured animals which are not appropriate as a means of transport or as beasts of burden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variety and assortment of God's favors bears witness to His providence, mercy, and blessing.
rows.anchor: favours is their variety and assortment, which bears evidence to His providence, mercy and blessing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variety of quadrupeds is further evidence of monotheism and the hereafter, meant to prompt reflection.
rows.anchor: The same evidence is pointed out here through the variety found in quadruped animals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The duty to benefit from livestock includes the previously stated duty to share its due, which context makes clear without repetition.
rows.anchor: there was no need to repeat it here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against Satan addresses his effort to lead people into self-made rules of permissibility and to sacrifice God's livestock to idols.
rows.anchor: regard things lawful and unlawful of their own selves and offer and sacrifice quadruped animals blessed to them before idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's two attacks here are polytheistic whispering and, in the preceding passage, wasteful spending; both have proved effective.
rows.anchor: both these types of onslaughts of Satan have proven to be very effective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The terms for eating and provision carry broad senses: what is benefited from or used, and God's sustenance.
rows.anchor: the former implies what is benefited and used and the latter to God’s sustenance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He construes the accusative for “eight” as governed by an omitted imperative, while others generally posit an omitted past-tense verb.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, the occasion demands the suppression of an imperative verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic word for a pair can also denote one member of that pair, as shown in Qur'anic and classical Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: it is also used to denote one member of a pair

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four domesticated kinds whose milk and meat Arabs consumed were goats, rams, cows, and camels; “anʿām” can also include wild quadrupeds when annexed to “beasts.”
rows.anchor: Amongst the domesticated animals in Arabia, there were four whose milk and meat were consumed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs disputed which domestic animals were lawful, the Prophet is told to question Quraysh and demand logical or scriptural proof grounded in Abraham's religion.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has asked the Prophet (sws) to take one member of each of them and inquire from the Quraysh about their lawfulness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Counting male and female members gives eight; the question exposes the inconsistency of allowing an animal while banning some of its parts or gendered uses, contrary to nature and reason.
rows.anchor: Human nature and intellect entail that if a tree is lawful, then its fruit should also be lawful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Valid proof would be scriptural evidence from Abraham or natural reasoning; ancestral custom, the Arabs' argument in 6:148, is neither.
rows.anchor: this is neither logical evidence nor scriptural one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an counters Arab animal taboos with Torah evidence from Abraham's life and logical, natural arguments for monotheism, unlike appeals to forefathers.
rows.anchor: the complete written evidence from Abraham’s life found in the Torah every word of which bears witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asking whether the Arabs witnessed God's prohibition exposes that they have neither reason nor revelation for attributing these taboos to Him.
rows.anchor: Were they present when God forbade them?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unjust are Quraysh's religious leaders, who fabricate prohibitions to mislead others; their false campaign will fail, promising success for the Islamic mission.
rows.anchor: The people who are implied to here are the religious leaders of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's proclamation addresses animals forbidden under Abraham's religion in the debate with Arab polytheists; it concerns quadrupeds in context, not a complete list of Islamic prohibitions.
rows.anchor: here since the context relates to quadruped animals only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inclusive phrase about anyone who eats refutes pagan distinctions that restricted particular animals to certain people or to men rather than women.
rows.anchor: just as their polytheistic sacrifices are baseless, this discrimination in their consumption too is fictitious

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Carrion, poured blood, and pork are prohibited for outward impurity; the singular pronoun applies to each separately, while slaughter in another's name is inward impurity through polytheism and disobedience.
rows.anchor: The prohibition of the first three of these is because of their apparent filth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrahamic lawfulness and unlawfulness rest on both divine command and human nature and intellect; the necessity exception is discussed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: they are also based on human nature and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's religion permits all pure, wholesome things and forbids impure ones; Islam follows this principle because it is based on Abraham's religion.
rows.anchor: all pure and wholesome things were lawful and all impure ones were unlawful ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israelites were additionally forbidden some wholesome foods as punishment for rebellion; these restrictions no longer apply in Islam, and Jews had been promised their removal through God's final messenger.
rows.anchor: some pure and wholesome things too were forbidden to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah passages describe a ban on animal fat; the Qur'anic exception covers fat inseparable from meat or attached to the back, intestines, or bone, while the Torah's absolute restriction appears to be a rabbinic addition.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this harsh and strict view is actually of the rabbis and scholars of the Jews

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since some blood remains attached to meat, the phrase “blood poured forth” limits the restriction to natural bounds.
rows.anchor: the expression “blood poured

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promised in Sūrah al-Māʾidah that accepting the final messenger would lift Israelite burdens because he would restore Abraham's natural religion.
rows.anchor: if they profess faith in the last messenger, these burdens would be lifted from them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's emphasis that He is truthful also implies that Jewish and Christian opponents are lying about Abraham's religion and Israelite law.
rows.anchor: it also indicates that His adversaries are liars

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning addresses both Quraysh and Israelites: God's vast mercy grants stubborn wrongdoers respite, but does not avert their eventual punishment.
rows.anchor: It does delay God’s punishment but does not ward off His established practice regarding wrongdoers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters invent prohibitions without evidence, while Jewish prohibitions punished rebellion; Islam lifts both extremes and allows what is pure according to nature and reason.
rows.anchor: This religion is devoid of the innovations of the Idolaters and the extremities of the Jews

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foundational Islamic rule is that wholesome things are lawful and impure things unlawful; the Qur'an describes the Prophet as lifting previous burdens and restrictions.
rows.anchor: He directs them to do good, forbids them from evil, regards pure things as lawful to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes that the nails of animals that do not hunt have a term in contrast with the claws of those that do.
rows.anchor: that do not hunt are called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jewish law allowed quadrupeds only if they had split hooves and chewed cud; the term for animals with nails refers to intact hooves, so camels and rabbits were forbidden to Jews despite being lawful in Abraham's religion.
rows.anchor: among the Jews, only those quadruped animals were lawful which had split hooves and which chewed the cud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These food restrictions punished Israelite rebellion rather than reflecting inherent impurity; repeated questioning and evasions made their law burdensome, described as “burdens and shackles” at 7:157.
rows.anchor: animals with nails and the fat were not unlawful to the Jews because they had some intrinsic reason for prohibition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites also had stricter restrictions on sea animals, allowing only fish with fins and scales, and prohibited waterfowl and other birds beyond hunting birds.
rows.anchor: sea animals having fins and scales were lawful and all the rest were forbidden
